title: O’Gara v. Equifax Information Services, LLC
lead: A son alleges that a credit bureau attached his father’s tax lien to his file. His discovery motion tests how evidence of other mixed files, internal procedures, and later matching reforms can bear on negligence and willfulness in his individual case.

actors.name: Charles Michael O’Gara III
actors.role: Consumer alleging that his father’s property-tax liability damaged his credit.

actors.name: Charles Michael O’Gara II
actors.role: Father whose lien was allegedly mixed into his son’s file.

actors.name: Equifax Information Services
actors.role: Credit-reporting defendant resisting portions of discovery.

actors.name: Magistrate Judge Matthew P. Brookman
actors.role: Judge resolving the motion to compel.

proceedings: After conferences and supplemental responses, O’Gara moved to compel further interrogatory and document responses.
The court granted the motion in part and denied it in part, requiring ordered supplementation within fourteen days and leaving each side its costs.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical docket-order brief without a fresh audit or current-rule certification. A disputed electronic-reporter citation is not repeated. Pinpoints are original numbered order pages. The order resolves discoverability, not liability, damages, or ultimate Rule 407 admissibility.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A shared name and address become part of an alleged credit-file error
paragraphs: Charles Michael O’Gara III alleged that, at eighteen while living with his father, he received records treating him as responsible for unpaid property taxes actually owed by Charles Michael O’Gara II. Father and son shared first and last names and the relevant address. He alleged credit denials from 2007 through 2015.

Equifax’s reproduced response said the lien appeared in June 2007 and was removed March 4, 2016 after his first dispute. O’Gara challenged matching by names without adequate unique identifiers such as birth date or Social Security number. He asserted Fair Credit Reporting Act § 1681e(b) reasonable-accuracy-procedure and § 1681g file-disclosure claims, alleging negligence or willfulness and seeking statutory and punitive damages, costs, and fees. These were unresolved claims, not established violations.

sections.title: Conferences and supplements leave a broad discovery disagreement
sections.cue: What standard did the court apply?
paragraphs: After repeated meetings and some supplemental answers, O’Gara sought more on matching procedures, his file, similar disputes and suits, studies, internal reports, and a New York Attorney General investigation and settlement. Equifax principally asserted irrelevance and disproportionality.

Magistrate Judge Matthew Brookman applied Rule 26(b)(1): nonprivileged relevance and proportionality considering issue importance, amount at stake, access, resources, usefulness, and burden compared with likely benefit. Discoverable information need not itself be admissible. Under Rule 37, O’Gara initially had to establish relevance, after which Equifax needed a particular justification for resisting the request.

sections.title: Definitions and existing answers narrow what must be supplied
sections.cue: Which broad inquiries were properly resisted?
paragraphs: O’Gara referred to mixed files “as defined herein” without providing the definition. The court found an ambiguity objection understandable but supplied meanings: a mixed file involved data matched to the wrong consumer, and a confirmed mixed file involved a dispute followed by confirmation of that mix. Affected answers had to be supplemented accordingly.

Several detailed procedure interrogatories were otherwise adequately answered through responses and manuals; O’Gara identified no specific deficiency. The court denied an accuracy-study request extending beyond public-record matching and lacking time limits, and another mixed-file study request covering all time. Reinvestigation inquiries under § 1681i were unsupported because no such claim or relevance explanation appeared.

Rule 26(a)(1) initial disclosure did not require an inventory of every electronically stored information system. But properly directed discovery could identify systems to plan electronic production. Requests identifying consumer-information and email systems were granted with necessary supplements; bankruptcy-specific systems were irrelevant to the tax-lien dispute.

sections.title: The individual file and similar incidents support targeted discovery
sections.cue: Why were generalized burden objections inadequate?
paragraphs: Equifax had supplied some dates and lien information but omitted how it determined mixing, the other consumer’s full identity and file identifier, the cause, who corrected it, and the correction information. Those details about O’Gara’s own file were plainly relevant and ordered. A separate mixed-file categorization inquiry was denied because relevance was unexplained and manuals substantially answered it.

Five-year counts of confirmed mixes, related lawsuits, and consumer disputes could show awareness of recurring defects and unreasonable procedures, supporting negligence or willfulness. Other incidents were not irrelevant simply because this plaintiff challenged one lien; even inadmissible complaints might lead to useful evidence.

Relevance did not end the proportionality analysis. Both sides’ cited verdicts involved different circumstances and did little to establish this case’s stakes. Equifax largely listed factors without evidence or concrete explanation of burden. That did not justify withholding the five-year interrogatory answers or internal mixed-file reports.

sections.title: Later matching reforms remain discoverable within a narrower scope
sections.cue: Why did the remedial-measures objection fail?
paragraphs: A New York Attorney General investigation produced a 2015 credit-reporting agreement, and a 2017 announcement described enhanced public-record matching standards for implementation later that year. O’Gara connected the same algorithms and institutional knowledge to his claims. Equifax said his lien was already gone and only few files were mixed. The court found a relevant link; low incidence did not erase relevance, and the announced changes would affect substantial tax-lien data.

The court adopted O’Gara’s narrowed request for mixed files involving his public-record problem rather than ordering the whole investigation. Two interrogatories, including whether his lien would appear under the new standard, were already fully answered. Remaining questions about reasons and intended effects, and related documents, had to be answered within the limit. Other ordered responses withholding information on the rejected investigation-relevance ground also required supplementation.

Equifax first raised subsequent-remedial-measures protection in supplemental responses about ninety days late, waiving that objection for discovery. Independently, Federal Rule of Evidence 407 admissibility was a different question from discovery relevance. The court neither declared the evidence admissible at trial nor made every late objection inexcusably waived in every setting.

sections.title: The mixed ruling carries no expense shift or merits judgment
sections.cue: What did the final order require?
paragraphs: On January 23, 2018, Brookman granted the motion in part and denied it in part, directing the ordered supplements within fourteen days. Each side bore its discovery-dispute costs under the discretionary mixed-result treatment of Rule 37(a)(5).

Equifax had conferred and supplemented, some requests were poorly drawn or inapplicable, and no discovery from an earlier disqualification phase was compelled here. The order awarded no statutory damages and decided no credit-reporting liability. No separate opinion, voting division, or appendix appeared.
